content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pods of the pea plant (Pisum sativum) harvested before the seeds fully mature. Raw peas have a fresh, slightly sweet flavor and a crisp texture. They can be eaten raw in salads, smoothies, or as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are ancestors of many cultivated pea varieties used in cooking.
Raw pods are rich in B‑vitamins, especially folate, which is important for cell division.
In ancient cultures peas symbolized abundance and fertility.
Peas fix nitrogen in the soil, improving its fertility.
Raw green peas are common in Asian cuisines, such as Japanese and Korean dishes.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Raw green peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Peas are abundant in vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, iron, and magnesium, which are essential for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Raw peas raise blood glucose slowly, beneficial for blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids in peas help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce the absorption of certain minerals; soaking peas before eating can mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas and gastrointestinal discomfort in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw green peas can be tossed into fresh salads, blended into smoothies, added to salsas, or enjoyed as a crunchy snack after a brief blanching. They can also be soaked and sprouted for pea shoots.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags at –18 °C; thaw and rinse quickly before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced coffee, brewed, decaffeinated is a refreshing beverage made from specially processed coffee beans that have had the caffeine removed. The preparation involves cold‑water extraction (cold brew) for 12–24 hours, after which the concentrate is chilled and served over ice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cold brew delivers a smoother, less bitter flavor profile compared with hot‑brewed coffee.
Decaffeination is usually performed by water‑process or CO₂ extraction, preserving most aromatic compounds.
Cold‑brew retains more antioxidants than hot coffee due to the long, low‑temperature steeping.
U.S. sales of decaf cold brew have grown over 30% in the past five years.
The drink is often served with milk, cream, or flavored syrups, but its pure taste shines best without additives.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: The lack of caffeine makes the beverage suitable for caffeine‑sensitive individuals and allows enjoyment of coffee flavor without sleep disruption.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cold brew preserves high levels of chlorogenic acids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Served cold and often unsweetened, it contributes to daily fluid intake.

items.title: May support heart health
items.content: Moderate coffee consumption, including decaf, has been linked to a reduced risk of cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Gentle on stomach
items.content: The absence of caffeine and lower acidity make it less irritating for sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Commercial products may contain sugar, flavorings, or preservatives that increase calories and could trigger allergies.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Although less acidic than hot coffee, the drink can still affect a very sensitive stomach if consumed in excess.

items.title: Storage safety
items.content: An opened bottle of cold brew can lose aroma quickly and become a breeding ground for bacteria if left at room temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the decaf cold brew over ice, add milk, plant‑based cream, or flavored syrup to taste. It also works as a base for cocktails, smoothies, or dessert sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the finished beverage refrigerated in a sealed container for up to 5–7 days. Flavor and aroma deteriorate over time; discard if it becomes sour or shows mold.

peas-and-carrots-frozen-cooked-no-added-.title: Peas and carrots, frozen, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots, frozen and ready to eat without added fat, are a blend of green peas and carrots that have been blanched and flash‑frozen. The process preserves most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh vegetables, and the product is ready for consumption after heating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peas and carrots are a common combination in baby foods because of their mild flavor and bright color.
Individual quick freezing (IQF) keeps vegetable cells intact, preventing large ice crystals from forming.
No added fat makes the product low‑calorie and suitable for weight‑management diets.
Carrots are an excellent source of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Peas provide a good amount of plant protein and fiber, contributing to satiety.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Carrots contain high levels of beta‑carotene, supporting vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Peas deliver a complete set of essential amino acids useful for muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, helps regulate blood sugar, and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes this product suitable for low‑calorie eating plans.

items.title: Contains vitamin C and folate
items.content: Both vegetables are good sources of vitamin C and folate, important for immune health and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to peas; discontinue use if allergic reactions occur.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain brands may add a small amount of salt during processing; check the label if you need a low‑sodium diet.

items.title: Vitamin loss over long storage
items.content: While freezing retains most nutrients, prolonged storage can lead to modest reductions in vitamin levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product can be heated in the microwave (2‑3 minutes) or briefly boiled (3‑4 minutes). Use it as a side dish, or add to soups, stews, pasta, rice dishes, or stir‑fries.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat pizza that differs from classic pepperoni is made with a thick crust (over 1.5 cm) and topped with a variety of meats – beef, chicken, ham, bacon or sausage. Tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese and aromatic herbs complete the flavor profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A thick crust retains the juiciness of the toppings and gives a more “bread‑like” bite.
Meat combos often use regional sausages, making each pizza unique in different areas.
Traditionally served in fast‑food restaurants, this pizza is also found in upscale pizzerias.
Combining several meats boosts protein content and makes the dish more filling.
Tomatoes are often roasted before being blended into the sauce, enhancing aroma.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Iron content
items.content: Beef and chicken contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella supplies calcium that supports bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and tomato sauce are good sources of B6 and B12 vitamins, important for the nervous system.

items.title: Energy density
items.content: Carbohydrates from the crust combined with protein from the meat provide sustained satiety.

items.title: High calorie count
items.content: Thick crust and meat toppings make the pizza calorie‑dense; moderation is advised.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Bacon and processed sausages can contain significant saturated fat, which should be considered in a heart‑healthy diet.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Meat products are often salty; people with hypertension should choose lower‑salt options.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into wedges. Optional toppings include fresh vegetables, basil, or a drizzle of olive oil. For a lighter meal, eat a portion of pizza and complement it with a salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the crust crisp.
